q: Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, is classified as:
x: Cyclohexane has a closed ring of carbon atoms only, with no benzene-type delocalised ring, so it is alicyclic (homocyclic, non-aromatic). Calling every six-membered ring aromatic is the tempting slip.

q: Which order shows the types of coal in increasing carbon content?
x: Coal forms over long periods of heat and pressure; the older and more compressed it is, the more carbon it has: peat (lowest), lignite, bituminous coal, then anthracite (about 90% or more). Writing the order backwards is the usual slip.

q: Catalytic cracking of heavy petroleum fractions is usually carried out at about 500 °C over:
x: Catalytic cracking uses a silica–alumina (zeolite) catalyst, which allows large molecules to be broken at a lower temperature and pressure than thermal cracking. Nickel is a hydrogenation catalyst, and V₂O₅ and promoted iron belong to the contact and Haber processes.

q: In catalytic reforming, n-hexane, C₆H₁₄, is converted into benzene, C₆H₆. How many moles of hydrogen are released per mole of hexane?
x: C₆H₁₄ → C₆H₆ + xH₂; hydrogen balance: 14 = 6 + 2x, so x = 4 (ring closure removes one H₂ and forming three C=C removes three more). Thinking of only the three double bonds gives 3; using H atoms instead of H₂ molecules gives 8.

q: A petrol sample knocks in an engine exactly like a mixture of 85% iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) and 15% n-heptane by volume. Its octane number is:
x: The octane number is the percentage of iso-octane (rated 100) in the iso-octane–n-heptane (rated 0) mixture that knocks like the fuel, so it is 85. Giving the heptane percentage, 15, is the slip.

q: In the fractional distillation of crude oil, which of these fractions is collected at the lowest temperature?
x: Fractions with smaller molecules have weaker dispersion forces and boil lower: petrol (about C₅–C₁₀) distils first, then kerosene, diesel oil and lubricating oil. Kerosene is the nearest fraction and the tempting mix-up.

q: The functional group –CONH₂ is found in:
x: –CONH₂ is a carbonyl group bonded to nitrogen, the amide group (e.g. ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂). Amines have –NH₂ without the C=O, which makes them the tempting confusion.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain has five carbons; numbering from the left puts the methyl groups on C-2 and C-3 (from the right they would be 3 and 4), so the name is 2,3-dimethylpentane. A branch named as ethyl or isopropyl means the longest chain was not chosen.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃C≡CCH(CH₃)CH₃ is:
x: The main chain has five carbons; numbering from the left gives the triple bond the lower locant (C-2) and puts the methyl on C-4, so 4-methylpent-2-yne. Numbering from the other end gives 2-methylpent-3-yne, which wrongly gives the branch priority over the triple bond.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂OH is:
x: The OH group is the principal group (suffix -ol) and gets the lowest number, so C-1 is the CH₂OH carbon and the double bond is between C-2 and C-3: prop-2-en-1-ol. Giving the double bond the lower number gives prop-1-en-3-ol, the most tempting wrong name.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COCl is:
x: –COCl is an acid (acyl) chloride group; with three carbons including the C=O carbon, the name is propanoyl chloride. Propyl chloride is CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl, which has no carbonyl group.

q: Which compound is a secondary alcohol?
x: In butan-2-ol the carbon bearing OH is bonded to two other carbons, so it is secondary. The propanol and butan-1-ol given are primary (one C attached), and (CH₃)₃COH is tertiary (three C attached).

q: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl and CH₃CHClCH₃ are examples of:
x: Both have the same carbon chain and the same functional group; only the position of the Cl on the chain differs, so they are position isomers. The carbon skeleton is unchanged, which rules out chain isomerism.

q: Which pair are chain isomers?
x: Butane and 2-methylpropane have the same formula C₄H₁₀ but different carbon skeletons (straight and branched), so they are chain isomers. Ethanol/methoxymethane and propanal/propanone are functional group isomers, and but-2-ene/but-1-ene are position isomers.

q: Propanone exists in equilibrium with a small amount of its enol form: CH₃COCH₃ ⇌ CH₂=C(OH)CH₃. This type of isomerism is called:
x: Keto and enol forms differ by the movement of an H atom and a double bond and change into each other in a dynamic equilibrium; this is tautomerism. Metamerism involves different alkyl groups on either side of the same functional group, as in ethers.

q: How many of these compounds show cis–trans isomerism: pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, 1,2-dichloroethene and propene?
x: Pent-2-ene (CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃) and 1,2-dichloroethene (ClCH=CHCl) have two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon, so they show it. 2-Methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, has two CH₃ on one carbon and propene has two H on one carbon, so they do not. Counting 2-methylbut-2-ene because it is a but-2-ene gives 3.

q: Which statement about cis- and trans-1,2-dichloroethene is correct?
o: The trans isomer has a net dipole moment and the higher boiling point
Both have the same boiling point because they have the same molecular formula
Both have zero dipole moment because they have the same bonds
The cis isomer has a net dipole moment and the higher boiling point
x: In the cis isomer both C–Cl dipoles point to the same side and add up, so it is polar and boils higher (about 60 °C); in the trans isomer they point opposite ways and cancel (about 48 °C). Thinking the more symmetrical trans form is more polar is the slip.

q: How many chiral carbon atoms (each bonded to four different groups) are present in CH₃CH(OH)CH(Cl)CH₃?
x: C-2 carries CH₃, OH, H and CH(Cl)CH₃, and C-3 carries CH₃, Cl, H and CH(OH)CH₃, so both are chiral; the end CH₃ carbons have three identical H atoms. Spotting only the carbon with OH gives 1.

q: Which species is a nucleophile?
x: A nucleophile donates an electron pair; NH₃ has a lone pair on nitrogen. BF₃, NO₂⁺ and CH₃⁺ are electron-deficient electron-pair acceptors, i.e. electrophiles.

q: In the methyl carbanion, CH₃⁻, the carbon atom is:
o: sp² hybridised, with a trigonal planar shape
sp³ hybridised, with a pyramidal shape
sp hybridised, with a linear shape
sp³ hybridised, with a square planar shape
x: The carbanion carbon has three bond pairs and one lone pair, four electron domains, so it is sp³ and pyramidal like NH₃. sp² and planar describes the carbocation CH₃⁺, which has no lone pair; that is the usual mix-up.

q: Bromoethane is heated with alcoholic KOH: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O. This is an example of:
x: H and Br are removed from neighbouring carbons and a C=C double bond forms, so it is elimination (dehydrohalogenation). With aqueous KOH the OH would replace Br instead, giving ethanol by substitution, which is the tempting answer.

q: Bromoethane is warmed with aqueous NaOH: CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻. This reaction is classified as:
x: The OH⁻ ion, an electron-pair donor, attacks the partly positive carbon of the C–Br bond and replaces Br⁻, so it is nucleophilic substitution. The reagent is a nucleophile, not an electrophile, and no double bond forms or is used.

q: 2-Methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH, reacts with chlorine in light by free-radical substitution. How many different monochloro products, C₄H₉Cl, can form?
x: The molecule has two kinds of hydrogen: nine equivalent H on the three CH₃ groups, giving (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl, and one H on the central carbon, giving (CH₃)₃CCl. So 2 products. Counting the three CH₃ groups as different gives 4.

q: Heterolytic fission of a covalent bond is favoured when:
o: The bond is non-polar and the reaction is in sunlight
The reaction is in the gas phase at very high temperature
The bond is polar and the reaction is in a polar solvent
x: Heterolysis gives ions, which are stabilised by a polar solvent, and it occurs most easily when the bond is already polar, such as C–Br. Light, high temperature in the gas phase and peroxides favour homolysis into free radicals.
